"They which shall be accounted worthy to obtain that world, and the resurrection from the dead, neither marry, nor are given in marriage: Neither can they die any more: for they are equal unto the angels; and are the children of God" (cf. Lk 20:35-36). And the Apostle said: "There is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus" (Gal 3:28).

St. Aphrahat * Do you not hear Moses when he says: "You forsook God who begot you" (Deut 32:15) LXX? Do you not hear Malachi rebuking them and saying that "one God created you" and there is "one Father of all" (Mal 2:10) LXX.

St. John Chrysostom * This is God's tenderness toward mankind, that He who is the Creator became afterward, according to grace, a Father to them also. He becomes so when the people, His creation, receive Him in their hearts, as the Apostle says: "the Spirit of his Son crying, Abba, Father." These are those who, receiving the Word, obtain from Him authority to become children of God, though by nature they are His creatures, unlike the receiving of the Spirit of the true natural Son. Therefore "the Word was made flesh," that He might make men fit for divinity. The same meaning can be obtained from the prophet Malachi, who says: "Hath not one God created us? have we not all one father?" (Mal 2:10). He put "created" first and then "father," to show, like the other writers, that from the beginning we were creatures by nature. God is our Creator by the Word, but afterward God the Creator became our Father also.

St. Athanasius the Apostolic * The Scripture declares the truth, saying: "First of all, believe that there is one God, who created and completed all things, and brought all things from non-being into being," He who contains all things, and Himself is contained by no one. Rightly Malachi also said among the prophets: "Hath not one God created us?" The Apostle also says in agreement with this: "One God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in you all" (Eph 4:6). So also the Lord says: "All things are delivered unto me of my Father" (Mt 11:27). It is clear that it is by the One who created all things, since things were not delivered to Him from another, but from what is His own.
St. Irenaeus

11 Judah hath dealt treacherously, and an abomination is committed in Israel and in Jerusalem; for Judah hath profaned the holiness of the LORD which he loved, and hath married the daughter of a strange god. 12 The LORD will cut off the man that doeth this, the master and the scholar, out of the tabernacles of Jacob, and him that offereth an offering unto the LORD of hosts. 13 And this have ye done again, covering the altar of the LORD with tears, with weeping, and with crying out, insomuch that he regardeth not the offering any more, or receiveth it with good will at your hand.
But ye are departed out of the way; Judah hath dealt treacherously, and an abomination is committed in Israel and in Jerusalem.
For Judah hath profaned the holiness of the LORD which he loved, and hath married the daughter of a strange god. [11]

The prophet repeats the word "treachery" and its derivatives five times in this passage [10-16], as though treachery had become a common mark of their life and conduct. The psalmist says: "Let them be ashamed which transgress without cause" (Ps 25:3). He also says: "be not merciful to any wicked transgressors" (Ps 59:5), "I beheld the transgressors, and was grieved; because they kept not thy word" (Ps 119:158). "But the wicked shall be cut off from the earth, and the transgressors shall be rooted out of it" (Prov 2:22), "the perverseness of transgressors shall destroy them" (Prov 11:3). Thus we see how grave is treachery and unfaithfulness to the covenant.
* So Paul lamented the Jews (for their treachery), and the Lord grieved over Jerusalem, and the divine Jeremiah lamented the people for their failure to fulfill the Law.

* I have sufficient ground S for hope in those who believe in You and enjoy Your help. For You are accustomed to show Your care for them, while You refute those who deal treacherously. It is fitting now to point out that it is not sinners but those who break the Law without cause (in treachery) whom shame covers. Not everyone sins in the same way, for some grieve because of certain circumstances or natural weakness, and others boast of their disobedience and contempt.

Theodorus, bishop of Cyrus Treachery here means betrayal of the covenant, for whoever breaks the covenant with God is treacherous and unfaithful in his covenant. This treachery is reflected in his dealings even with the one closest to him, the husband or wife whom he received from God as the partner of his life and a helper to him in all aspects of his life.

The sign of the treachery and the abomination is that they insulted their God by marrying pagan women [11] and divorcing their believing wives. He counted these two crimes as directed against Him personally, and as treachery against Him. The first crime is fellowship with unbelievers, where the unbeliever pushes the other party to deny the faith. The second crime is the dissolving of the holy marriage bond that God bound.

* If you wish to see more clearly how a Christian woman may by no means marry a Gentile, observe what the Apostle himself says: "The wife is bound by the law as long as her husband liveth; but if her husband be dead, she is at liberty to be married to whom she will; only in the Lord" (1 Cor 7:39), that is, to be a Christian. He who permits a second and a third marriage in the Lord forbids first marriages with a Gentile. For this reason Abraham also made his servant swear on his thigh, that is, by Christ who came from his seed, that he would not bring a foreign woman as wife for his son Isaac (Gen 24:1-9). And Ezra, when he discovered disobedience to God of this kind, made his countrymen put away their wives (Ezra 10:1-17). And the prophet Malachi speaks thus: "Judah hath dealt treacherously, and an abomination is committed in Israel and in Jerusalem; for Judah hath profaned the holiness of the LORD which he loved, and hath married the daughter of a strange god. The LORD will cut off the man that doeth this, the master and the scholar, out of the tabernacles of Jacob, and him that offereth an offering unto the LORD of hosts."
St. Jerome The LORD will cut off the man that doeth this, the master and the scholar, out of the tabernacles of Jacob, and him that offereth an offering unto the LORD of hosts. [12]

By such conduct, by which believers defile the holiness of the Lord, the believers cut off themselves and those who belong to them from the commonwealth of the people of God (Eph 2:12). The "master and the scholar" are also cut off, that is, the teachers and the learners, the blind leaders who fall, they and their followers, into the pit of error.

The believer who is married to a pagan is cut off "out of the tabernacles of Jacob," that is, from the people of God; and the priest who "offereth an offering unto the LORD" and commits the same fault falls under the same penalty: being cut off and deprived of the service of the temple of the Lord, and of his priesthood.

Because of the people's fornication with the daughters of Moab, who invited the people to idolatrous worship (Num 25:1), Israel joined itself to Baal-peor, and the Lord's anger was kindled against Israel. So Moses killed all the heads of the people who had committed this iniquity. Phinehas the high priest was also zealous with the zeal of God and thrust through with his spear the man who boldly joined himself to a Midianite woman, and the woman. In the same way Nehemiah drove out the grandson of the high priest because he had married a pagan woman (Neh 13:8).
The priest Phinehas, in this zeal of his, became a type of the Lord Christ, who delivered Himself to death on the Cross and so removed the divine wrath from those who believe in Him.

* If Phinehas, by his zeal in killing the evildoer, appeased the wrath of God, does not Jesus, who did not slay another but "gave himself a ransom for all" (1 Tim 2:6), take away the wrath of God against humanity?

St. Cyril of Jerusalem * If we are conformed to His death, sin certainly becomes a lifeless corpse in us, by the spear of Baptism, just like the adulterer who was cast down through the zeal of Phinehas.

St. Gregory of Nyssa And this have ye done again, covering the altar of the LORD with tears, with weeping, and with crying out, insomuch that he regardeth not the offering any more, or receiveth it with good will at your hand. [13]

In order to marry pagan women, the believers divorced their wives to make room for achieving their own desires. Even the men who did not divorce their believing wives treated them bitterly because of their attachment to the pagan women. The wives had nothing left but to complain with tears and the cry of a bitter heart, so the altar was covered with these bitter tears. Worship in the Temple, especially on feast days, turned into grief and tears instead of rejoicing in the Lord.

The offerings and sacrifices were no longer the delight of the Lord, because they ascended floating in the tears of the wives who were overpowered and wronged, and their cries rose out of them, just as the blood of Abel cried out silently against Cain!

Perhaps marriage to pagan women corrupted the concepts of worship, so that instead of the sacrifice being linked with praise and spiritual joy, it was linked with shouting and with a man cutting his body with swords and lances until the blood gushed out on the altar (1 Kgs 18:28). As the prophet Ezekiel says: "There sat women weeping for Tammuz" (Ezek 8:14).

Instead of worshiping with their believing wives in joy and praises, so that their prayers and their offerings lifted up with pure hands would not be hindered, the men resorted to pagan wives and worshiped with them in a spirit of gloom.

Perhaps the tears and wailing here are because these treacherous men felt their error, so they offer tears without abandoning their attachment to the pagan women. They practice the worship of God to satisfy their consciences, and they practice pagan worship because of their attachment to the pagan women. They mix light with darkness. As Elijah the prophet said: "How long halt ye between two opinions? if the LORD be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him" (1 Kgs 18:21). And the Apostle Paul says: "For what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness? And what concord hath Christ with Belial? or what part hath he that believeth with an infidel?" (2 Cor 6:14-15)

* "What communion hath light with darkness?" Where there is distinction and an irreconcilable opposition between light and darkness, whoever shares in both has a portion in neither, because of the opposition between the two parts, each against the other, at the same time in his life, which is a mixture of the two. By his faith he draws on the part that gives light, but by his dark habits he extinguishes the lamp of the mind. Since it is impossible for light and darkness to be in fellowship together, the person who embraces both is an enemy to himself, being divided against himself, divided between the two ways of virtue and evil. He sets up within himself a battle between opposites. And since, when there are two enemies, both cannot be victorious, and the victory of one leads to the death of the opponent, this civil war causes disturbance in his life. And the stronger side cannot prevail unless the other is completely destroyed.
St. Gregory of Nyssa

entries.section: 6. Breaking the covenant with the wife:

paragraphs.text: 14 Yet ye say, "Wherefore?" Because the LORD hath been witness between thee and the wife of thy youth, against whom thou hast dealt treacherously: yet is she thy companion, and the wife of thy covenant. 15 And did not he make one? Yet had he the residue of the spirit. And wherefore one? That he might seek a godly seed. Therefore take heed to your spirit, and let none deal treacherously against the wife of his youth. 16 "For the LORD, the God of Israel, saith that he hateth putting away: for one covereth violence with his garment, saith the LORD of hosts: therefore take heed to your spirit, that ye deal not treacherously."
Yet ye say, Wherefore?
Because the LORD hath been witness between thee and the wife of thy youth, against whom thou hast dealt treacherously: yet is she thy companion, and the wife of thy covenant. [14]

Again, the men behaved with a spirit of treachery and betrayal, for they married pagan women or took them as concubines, so that these would share with the wives their rights in their husbands' hearts, and also enjoy a fitting standard of living. This shameful conduct will not bring peace and joy, but inward gloom and distress.

God cares for the family; in the marriage contract He counts Himself a witness to it, so whoever dissolves this bond is like one who has broken a pledge to which God Himself bears witness. Every betrayal of this pledge has the Lord Himself as its witness. And whoever keeps the pledge with sincerity of heart and fitting conduct is counted faithful in the things of God.
He calls her "the wife of thy youth," since he loved her in his youth, so why does he ignore this love and esteem for her in his old age?

He also calls her "thy companion," that is, one who shares with him in her husband's joys and sorrows; they share together in managing all the affairs of the family, she feels responsibility with him, and she supports him as a helper to him.

"The wife of thy covenant," that is, the husband was bound to her with a firm bond, and she entered with him into a binding covenant in the most minute matters, so it is fitting for both to fulfill what they pledged.
And did not he make one? Yet had he the residue of the spirit.
And wherefore one? That he might seek a godly seed.

entries.section: 6. Breaking the covenant with the wife:

paragraphs.text: Therefore take heed to your spirit, and let none deal treacherously against the wife of his youth. [15]

He gives us the reasons that oblige the spouses to live together to the end in holy love, esteem, and peace. God created one Eve for one Adam, so that man would not think of another wife. As it is written in the book of Leviticus: "Neither shalt thou take a wife to her sister, to vex her, to uncover her nakedness, beside the other in her lifetime" (Lev 18:18).

God could have created another Eve, but He wanted Adam to be occupied with "seeking a godly seed," that is, to have holy children who bear the image of God. What occupies him is not the lusts of the body, to satisfy them with this woman and that, but the establishing of a holy home in which there is mutual respect in the Lord and faithfulness in love, without one betraying the other by giving his feelings to someone else. This is the natural Law and the divine Law, that "every man have his own wife" (1 Cor 7:2), living together in chastity and purity, in a holy family, bringing forth offspring that worships God" (Ps 22:30). Thus "the bed [is] undefiled" (Heb 13:4).

* In the Gospel of Matthew He says: "Whosoever shall put away his wife, saving for the cause of fornication, causeth her to commit adultery" (Mt 5:32). He who marries a woman divorced from her husband is also counted as one who has committed adultery. In any case, the Creator does not allow those whom He joined to be separated except for the cause of fornication. Moses himself, in another passage, lays down a law that a man who marries a girl after violating her by force has no right to put away his wife (Deut 22:28-29). Now if the compulsory marriage that takes place after the use of violence remains forever, how much more the voluntary marriage, which is the fruit of agreement! This is the law of the prophet: "Do not leave the wife of thy youth." Thus you see Christ naturally following the way of the Creator in every place, whether in permitting divorce or forbidding it. You see Him also protecting marriage, whatever way you flee to. He forbids divorce, since He wants marriage not to be violated, and He permits divorce when marriage is stained by unfaithfulness. It befits you to be ashamed when you refuse to unite those whom your Christ unites.

* I draw your attention to the law of one wife. The very origin of the human race in the book of Genesis establishes this (Gen 1:27). It is very clear that God ordained this (one wife) from the beginning as a pattern for the generations that followed. For after He created Adam and saw the necessity of providing a helper for him, He took one rib from his ribs (Gen 2:21-22). He appointed for the man one woman only.

* Where shall we find language able to express fittingly the happiness of that marriage which the Church binds, which the offering confirms, which the blessing ordains and seals, which the angels celebrate, and which the Father approves? For young people on all the earth have no right to marry without the consent of their parents. What kind of yoke is this of two believers who share together one hope, one desire, one discipline, and one service? They enjoy kinship in the Spirit and in the flesh. They are fellow servants together, without conflict in their concerns. Rightly they are two in one flesh (Gen 2:24; Mt 19:5; Eph 5:31). Where the flesh is one, the spirit is also one. They pray together, fast together, teach together in fellowship, beseech together, and lift up their hands together. In the Church of God they occupy an equal place (Rom 12:15; 15:6; Gal 3:28; 1 Cor 12:12). They stand equally at the table of God, in troubles, in the face of persecutions, and in their refreshment. Neither hides anything from the other, neither ignores the other, and neither causes trouble to the other.

Tertullian the Scholar * Do not count it lawful to leave, after marriage, her who is without blemish. For He says: "Take heed to your spirit, and let none deal treacherously against the wife of his youth, for she is the partner of your life, and the remnant of your spirit. I, and no other, have made her" (cf. Mal 2:14-15). The Lord says: "What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder" (Mt 19:6).
The Didascalia For the LORD, the God of Israel, saith that he hateth putting away: for one covereth violence with his garment, saith the LORD of hosts.

entries.section: 6. Breaking the covenant with the wife:

paragraphs.text: Therefore take heed to your spirit, that ye deal not treacherously. [16]

What is truly grave is the attempt to hide their evil conduct and the treachery and betrayal in their hearts by pretending before others that they love their wives and show kindness to them, and cover them with their garments. They hide their evils and their injustice as with a garment.
God permitted the Jews to divorce because of the hardness of their hearts (Mt 19:8), but He hates it, especially since they were allowing "a man to put away his wife for every cause" (Mt 19:3).

The prophet affirms that in divorcing a wife for any cause, and in marrying a second while the first is alive, there is treachery, not only against the first wife, but it is a crime of treachery directed against God, who established the Law of holy marriage.
The Lord Christ came to raise the believers to the level of spiritual maturity and serious responsibility, so that a man would not divorce his wife except for the cause of fornication.
St. Augustine comments on the words of the Lord concerning not divorcing, saying:

[The Mosaic law did not command divorce, but commanded the one who divorces his wife to give her a certificate of divorce, because in giving her a certificate of divorce there is something that calms the rage of a man's anger.

For the Lord, who commanded those of hardened heart to give a certificate of divorce, indicated that He did not wish for divorce as far as possible. Therefore when the Lord Himself was asked about this matter, He answered, saying: "Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you" (Mt 19:8), for however great the hardness of heart of him who wishes to divorce his wife, when he knows that by means of the certificate of divorce she can marry another, his anger subsides and he does not divorce her.

And to confirm this principle, that a wife is not to be divorced lightly, the Lord of glory made the only exception the cause of fornication. He commanded that all the other troubles be endured with steadfastness for the sake of conjugal love and for the sake of chastity, and the Lord of glory confirmed the same principle by calling the one who marries a divorced woman an "adulterer."]
Ye have wearied the LORD with your words.
Yet ye say, Wherein have we wearied him?
When ye say, Every one that doeth evil is good in the sight of the LORD, and he delighteth in them;
or, Where is the God of judgment? [17]

He says: "Ye have wearied the LORD with your words." They offered excuses and justifications for their sinful conduct, as though they did not recognize their grievous faults. The holy God, who desires His people to be holy, as holy children, grieves over them because of their lack of discernment, for they count evil as good work, and think that whatever they do, they are the delight of God. And if He is angry at their conduct, which in their eyes is good, they ascribe to God injustice and lack of fairness.
How astonishing! Man stands in the position of the judge, not only to judge his brother, but even to judge God Himself, saying: "Where is the God of judgment?"
Make the believer a holy leader!
* You created everything for the sake of man, and You made him a head and a king, with authority.
You desire every person to be a holy leader!
* For man's sake You established much, and by his fall You cursed the earth, and it brought forth thorns and thistles!
You desire every believer to be a secret of blessing to many.
Because of Joseph You blessed the house of Potiphar, his master.
And for the sake of David Your servant You blessed Solomon.
And because of Jonah the fugitive nature was stirred up, and the sailors lost their provisions and their peace, and almost lost their very lives.
Sanctify me and draw me to You, O Holy One.
Draw many to You by Your Holy Spirit.
* Grant me not to betray Your covenant, but let it be to me a secret of life and peace.
By Your new covenant You grant me resurrection from death, and bestow on me peace at the level of heaven!
* Let Your commandment be the constitution of my life, and Your word ever on my lips, that I may enjoy the knowledge of You, and bear witness to it by the power of the Spirit.
* Grant me not to betray my brethren, but to be faithful to You in my relationship with my brethren and my family.
Dwell in the midst of Your Church which is in my heart, and be manifested in the church of my home!
* Take away from me all treachery against the covenant, cleanse me of every abomination, and let Your Kingdom be established within me, that I may be wholly Yours, and live as befits a son of Yours.
And I commit myself to respond to Your Holy Spirit.

entries.section: 1. Preparing for the coming of the Messiah:

paragraphs.text: 1 "Behold, I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me: and the Lord, whom ye seek, shall suddenly come to his temple, even the messenger of the covenant, whom ye delight in: behold, he shall come, saith the LORD of hosts."
In contempt the wicked were asking: "Where is the God of judgment?" (Mal 2:17). The answer came at once: He will come in the fullness of time, and this was now at the doors.
Behold, I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me.
And the Lord, whom ye seek, shall suddenly come to his temple, even the messenger of the covenant, whom ye delight in.
Behold, he shall come, saith the LORD of hosts. [1]

The Lord refers to St. John the Baptist, whom He sends before Him to prepare the way for Him by proclaiming repentance, offering the baptism of repentance, and bearing witness to the Lord as the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.

He calls St. John His messenger (angel). Here many of the Fathers of the Church stand in amazement before God's surpassing love for man, for He desires to call every person His own messenger (angel). He is enamored of man and wants to raise him to the highest heavenly level.

God prepared humanity for His coming since the fall of Adam and Eve, when He gave them the promise: "I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel" (Gen 3:15). Then came the fathers and the prophets presenting types and prophecies about His coming, and finally God sends John the Baptist as a messenger (angel) to prepare the way for the promised Messiah, and God called him "my messenger" [1]. He comes to proclaim the divine message that he received from heaven and not from men. The Holy Bible was sealed with this promise, and the opening of the Gospel of our teacher the Apostle Mark, being the first of the Gospels to be written, bears witness to the fulfillment of this promise (Mk 1:12).

St. John the Baptist came to prepare the way before the Lord Christ by proclaiming repentance and offering the baptism of repentance. He came to declare to them that their salvation does not lie in their physical descent from Abraham the father of the fathers, but in the coming of Him whose coming Abraham hoped for.

This prophecy came perfectly clear, and it was fulfilled in the person of St. John the Baptist, who bore witness to Jesus Christ that He is "the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world" (Jn 1:29). For this reason the Jews tried to offer various interpretations of this text; some claimed that Malachi is speaking of himself as the messenger (angel) of the Lord, and others claimed that it refers to the angel of death who leads the wicked to cast them into the fire of Gehenna.

The prophet affirms that the Messiah, the Lord, comes suddenly to His temple, He whom the pious, those who fear the Lord, have sought since the days of Adam and Eve. They await Him with great joy, and as the Evangelist says, they were "waiting for the consolation of Israel" (Lk 2:25), and for redemption in Israel (Lk 2:38), for He is "the desire of all nations" (Hag 2:7). All find in Him the delight of their hearts.

"He shall suddenly come." His coming has drawn near, so we no longer wait for Him from afar as the patriarchs did, and the prophets after them, but the Messiah has come to be at the doors. Perhaps by "suddenly" he means that He will come at a time when many did not expect His coming, despite the clarity of the prophecies and the fixing of the date of His coming as given in the book of Daniel. Truly, at His birth the priests affirmed that He is born in Bethlehem Ephratah, but to them He came suddenly, since they were not prepared for His coming, although they knew this with their minds.

"To his temple": He came to the Temple in Jerusalem and cleansed it more than once of the sellers of doves and the moneychangers. He did this with authority, because it is His temple and His house. At the age of twelve He stood in the Temple in the midst of the teachers, drawing their hearts by His authority, for He was about His Father's business (Lk 2:49). And when He entered Jerusalem in the last week He went to the Temple directly (Mt 21:12). There the blind and the lame came to Him seeking healing (Mt 21:14). There He preached, debated, and performed signs and miracles.
Although He came to establish a new temple in the hearts of His believers, He honored the Temple in Jerusalem, demanding of us respect for the house of God.
"Behold, he shall come, saith the LORD of hosts," for the One who speaks is faithful in His promises and able to fulfill them; He has come and has not delayed.
* "There was a man sent from God, whose name was John" (Jn 1:6)... He was called "a messenger" (Mal 3:1), because the privilege of a messenger is that he says nothing of his own.

* Jesus spoke about John's clothing, his imprisonment, and his role in prophecy; by saying this He showed that he was greater than a prophet. What else does Jesus mean by his being greater? That he was very near to the One who was coming. He says: "Behold, I send my messenger before thy face," meaning his nearness to the Messiah. For as with kings, the one who rides beside the chariot is more famous than the rest, so it was with John, who appears in turn to be near to the very coming.

St. John Chrysostom * John is greater than the other prophets for the following reason: the other prophets prophesied about John that he was coming, but John pointed with his finger that He had truly come, saying: "Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world" (Jn 1:29). He did not merely reach the rank of a prophet, but the Baptist, by baptizing his Lord, was exalted. By this he fulfilled the prophecy of Malachi, who prophesied about a messenger (angel). John belonged to the order of the angels, not by nature, but because of the importance of his mission. It means that he is the messenger who announces the coming of the Lord.
St. Jerome * By the word "angels" (Gal 3:19) he means the messengers of God, that is, Moses, the son of Nun, and other prophets up to John the Baptist.

Father Ambrosiaster * In this text he foretells to us both comings of Christ, the first and the second. The first, where he says: "The Lord shall suddenly come to his temple." This refers to the body of Christ, of which He Himself said in the Gospel: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up" (Jn 2:19). And His second coming he prophesied in these words: "But who may abide the day of his coming? and who shall stand when he appeareth?"

* Men are called angels, for the Apostle says of himself: "Ye received me as an angel of God" (Gal 4:14). And it is said of John the Baptist: "Behold, I send my messenger before thy face, which shall prepare thy way before thee" (Mt 11:10). Therefore at His coming with all His angels (Mt 25:31), His saints will also be with Him.
St. Augustine

2 But who may abide the day of his coming? and who shall stand when he appeareth? for he is like a refiner's fire, and like fullers' soap: 3 And he shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver: and he shall purify the sons of Levi, and purge them as gold and silver, that they may offer unto the LORD an offering in righteousness.

The holy Lord comes to establish from humanity His holy temple. With His marvelous love for man and His esteem for him, and though He counts them as heavenly gold or silver, He does not accept that there be in him any dross or defilement. He desires to clothe him with His divine righteousness, so that his heart becomes a holy temple, and God smells in every worship or offering a sweet savor, the object of His divine delight.
But who may abide the day of his coming?
And who shall stand when he appeareth?
For he is like a refiner's fire, and like fullers' soap. [2]

Although He came incarnate in humility, to meet all classes, even the slaves who were despised at that time, yet "who may abide the day of his coming?" "Who shall stand when he appeareth?" He came not to judge but to save the world, and yet He was the One with authority before whom the Jewish leaders trembled.
This is about His first coming to save; what will it be at His last coming to judge? The believers see Him with eyes like doves, while the wicked look at Him with eyes burning with fire!
The Lord Christ came like the refiner's fire, like the fullers' soap (lye) that purifies and cleans cloths of the filth that clings to them. He came to send fire on the earth (Lk 12:49-50).

* Christ Himself, who did all this, will afterward stand before us as our Judge. Certainly the prophets did not pass over this, but prophesied about Him. Some saw Him in the very form in which He will be when He stands before us, and some prophesied only through words. Daniel was among the barbarians and the Babylonians when he saw Christ coming on the clouds. Listen to his words: "I saw, and, behold, one like the Son of man came with the clouds of heaven, and came to the Ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. And there was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all people, nations, and languages, should serve him" (cf. Dan 7:13-14). He pointed to the judgment of God and His verdict, saying: The thrones were set up, the books were opened. A fiery stream issued and came forth from before him. Thousands of thousands ministered unto him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him (Dan 7:9-10). Daniel did not declare this only, but showed the honor that the righteous receive when he said: "Judgment was given to the saints of the most High; and the time came that the saints possessed the kingdom" (Dan 7:22). This judgment will come through fire. Malachi said: "He is coming (like the fire of a refining furnace), like fullers' soap." Then the righteous will enjoy great honor. And Daniel speaks of the resurrection where he says: "Many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake" (Dan 12:12).

St. John Chrysostom * When we fell, the horn of salvation was raised up for us (Lk 1:69), and the chief cornerstone (Isa 28:16), who binds us to Himself and to one another, was laid at the right time, or the fire (Mal 3:2-3) arose which purifies our debased and evil matters (1 Cor 3:13-15).

St. Gregory of Nazianzus One of the Fathers of the Church says: [It is not presumptuous that John is called an angel though he is a man, because of his power and worthiness, for he is more glorious than if he were an angel in name or in nature. For an angel is called an angel because of his nature as an angel rather than because he has qualified for it. But it is a miraculous thing that a man, while in his human nature, passes over into angelic holiness and receives the grace of God which is not according to nature].
And he shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver:
And he shall purify the sons of Levi, and purge them as gold and silver, that they may offer unto the LORD an offering in righteousness. [3]

"He shall sit as a refiner," for He purifies humanity by His Gospel to establish from it a holy Church without blemish. He removes the dross from her, so she becomes pure gold refined by fire. The Apostle Paul says: "Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it; that he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word, that he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish" (Eph 5:25-27). And also: "Who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works..." (Titus 2:14).

"He shall purify the sons of Levi, and purge them as gold and silver." It is as though the Lord Christ purifies those who accepted to consecrate their lives to Him, for His praise and service and the offering of their hearts as living sacrifices, so that they become the spiritual sons of Levi of the New Testament.

Although the Lord Christ chose the disciples and the Apostles and gave them the gift of the priesthood, and their successors accordingly came to receive the same gift, yet there is a general priesthood that the believer receives in the sacrament of Baptism. Through it the believer offers his prayers, fasts, gifts, and service as spiritual offerings acceptable to God. St. John says in the name of the whole Church: "[He] hath made us kings and priests unto God and his Father" (Rev 1:6).
The Lord Christ purifies His believers by His fiery Holy Spirit "through manifold temptations: that the trial of your faith... might be found unto praise and honour and glory" (1 Pet 1:6-7).

By the work of the Holy Spirit in the hearts of the believers, "the offering up of the Gentiles... [is] acceptable, being sanctified by the Holy Ghost" (Rom 15:16). Thus they fulfill the words of the psalmist: "Offer the sacrifices of righteousness" (Ps 4:5). And the words of the Apostle Paul: "I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service" (Rom 12:1).

* Remove the defilement of their blasphemy that has come upon them, and cleanse with the breaths of holy purification the souls buried in the foul mire, so that dens of robbers may be turned into houses of prayer.

* If they know nothing of the mysteries and visions, but have formed their judgments only on their own present interests... their stupidity in understanding prophecy is great, and their envy in human affairs is great. Such stupidity and envy must be uprooted from our minds. It befits a man to be more fervent than fire in order to stand against such a company. This is the reason for which Christ said: "I am come to send fire on the earth; and what will I, if it be already kindled?" (Lk 12:49) and for this the Spirit appeared in (the form of) fire.

St. John Chrysostom * "He shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost, and with fire" (Mt 3:11)... The blessed Baptist added to the word "Spirit" the expression that carries the sense of action: "and with fire." This does not mean that we are baptized by Christ with fire, but that through the reference to fire the life-giving power of the Spirit is granted to us.
St. Cyril the Great

entries.section: 3. He changes them and is not changed:

paragraphs.text: 4 Then shall the offering of Judah and Jerusalem be pleasant unto the LORD, as in the days of old, and as in former years. 5 "And I will come near to you to judgment; and I will be a swift witness against the sorcerers, and against the adulterers, and against false swearers, and against those that oppress the hireling in his wages, the widow, and the fatherless, and that turn aside the stranger from his right, and fear not me, saith the LORD of hosts. 6 For I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed.
Then shall the offering of Judah and Jerusalem be pleasant unto the LORD, as in the days of old, and as in former years. [4]

In the first chapter he spoke of their unclean offerings upon His altar (Mal 1:7); here, as he speaks of the coming of the Messiah and the believers' enjoyment of His righteousness, he says: "The offering of Judah and Jerusalem [shall] be pleasant unto the LORD" [4].
He speaks here of the new offering through the Cross, and the sacrifice of the Eucharist, which is the delight of the Father and not hateful to the Lord.

"As in the days of old, and as in former years": here he takes their memory back to the offering of Abel which God accepted, and the sacrifice of Noah after the Flood which God smelled as a sweet savor, and the sacrifice of Aaron when He sent down fire from heaven, and also the sacrifice of Elijah, and so on. So through the Cross the Lord makes us accepted in Him and beloved (Eph 1:6), and He delights in us and in what we offer to Him of what He gave us. The Apostle says of his ministry among the Gentiles with the Gospel of salvation: "That the offering up of the Gentiles might be acceptable, being sanctified by the Holy Ghost" (Rom 15:16). The Apostle also asks us to offer a sacrifice acceptable to God through our union with the sacrifice of the Cross: "I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service" (Rom 12:1).

* How can the person who is conformed to this world, who has not been transformed by the renewing of his mind, and has not delighted in the newness of this life, but instead follows the life according to the old man, obey the Apostle, who commands you to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God? How can you, being a priest of God and anointed for this very purpose, offer an offering to God, not an offering entirely foreign to you or deceptive, as consisting of what is outside you, but one that truly seeks an offering which is yours, containing what is within you, the inner man in you, who helps you to be perfect and without blemish according to the word of the Lamb, having in him no wrath or blemish (Rom 8:9-11; 1 Cor 3:16-17; 2 Cor 13:5; Col 1:27)? How can you place these offerings before God if you do not listen to the Law that forbids any unholy man to be a priest?
St. Gregory of Nyssa * The Gentiles were offered to God as an acceptable sacrifice when they believed in Christ and were sanctified by the Gospel.

St. Augustine And I will come near to you to judgment; and I will be a swift witness against the sorcerers, and against the adulterers, and against false swearers, and against those that oppress the hireling in his wages,

entries.section: 3. He changes them and is not changed:

paragraphs.text: The widow, and the fatherless, and that turn aside the stranger from his right, and fear not me, saith the LORD of hosts. [5]

God, who has compassion on humanity as on His children, and receives them as His delight, and smells their gifts, from what He gave them, as a sweet savor of delight through the Cross, draws near to them to judge those who refuse to respond to His love and defy divine justice.

A. His witness by His Cross against the sorcerers: By His Cross He is a witness against the sorcerers who do not accept divine love, but trust in the power of their father the devil. At the close of the Holy Bible the Lord Himself warns against sorcery, and counts "sorcerers" among the groups whose portion is the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone, which is the second death, eternal (Rev 21:8).

B. His witness by His Cross against the adulterers who wallow in lusts. In the book of Isaiah the Lord rebukes the perverse people: "But draw near hither, ye sons of the sorceress, the seed of the adulterer and the whore" (Isa 57:3). And in Hosea: "Plead with your mother, plead: for she is not my wife, neither am I her husband: let her therefore put away her whoredoms out of her sight, and her adulteries from between her breasts" (Hos 2:2). "They are all adulterers, as an oven heated by the baker" (Hos 7:4).

* At the beginning of the prophecy he gave the city the name "harlot." "How is the faithful city become an harlot!" (cf. Isa 1:21). Thus he accuses them of adultery, not only by their breaking the sanctity of marriage, but also by breaking the commandments; while they seemed to be near to God, they were secretly slaves to the demons, and this in fact is flagrant adultery.

Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrus * She does not keep faithfulness in love toward me, but rather has betrayed intimacy and made light of the purity of union with me. And she has no desire to have the fruits of my will.

St. Cyril the Great C. His witness by His Cross against false swearers: Those who make light of the sanctity of God's name, and bear false witness. The Lord says in the prophet Zechariah: "It shall enter into the house of the thief, and into the house of him that sweareth falsely by my name: and it shall remain in the midst of his house, and shall consume it with the timber thereof and the stones thereof" (Hos 5:4).

D. His witness against those who wrong their brethren: They defraud the workers of their wages, crush the widow and the fatherless, and show no mercy to the stranger, depriving him of his rights because he does not know the law of the land. The Lord counted every action against these groups as a deprivation of the fear of the Lord and reverence for Him. The psalmist says of the wicked man: "There is no fear of God before his eyes" (Ps 36:1). God often warns us against practicing this injustice, counting that it is directed against Himself personally, and against His commandment. "Oppress not the widow, nor the fatherless, the stranger, nor the poor" (Zech 7:10). "Ye shall not afflict any widow, or fatherless child. If thou afflict them in any wise, and they cry at all unto me, I will surely hear their cry; and my wrath shall wax hot, and I will kill you with the sword" (Ex 22:22-24). "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world" (Jas 1:27).
* Those who have no protection are the more exposed to being victims of tyranny. The humbler the victim, the more the oppressor is counted as one who resists God.

St. Jerome St. Jerome sees in the widow the soul that has lost God as its heavenly Bridegroom, and in the fatherless the soul deprived of God's fatherhood, and in the stranger the soul that has no place in which to rest, that is, in the divine embrace, and the hireling is the one who is occupied with material things rather than eternal things. It befits us to care for such souls, and not to make light of their salvation, so that they may enjoy fellowship with God, and the sweetness of salvation, and the fellowship of eternal glory.

entries.section: 3. He changes them and is not changed:

paragraphs.text: For I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed. [6]

God shows His longsuffering toward them. Their fathers had rebelled against Him and His servants since their beginning as a nation in Egypt, where the Jews said to Moses: "Who made thee a prince and a judge over us?" (Ex 2:14); and after the Exodus, where the people murmured again and again against Moses and Aaron, and worshiped the golden calf. And even after entering the Promised Land, where they asked for themselves a king like all the nations (1 Sam 8:5), and the Lord said to Samuel the prophet: "They have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them" (1 Sam 8:7). Often they disobeyed the commandment, worshiped idols, and committed abominations. He says: "Even from the days of your fathers ye are gone away from mine ordinances, and have not kept them"]7[. He reveals to them that instead of returning to Him they have filled up the cup of their fathers' evil. As Ezra says: "Since the days of our fathers have we been in a great trespass unto this day" (Ezra 9:7).

He did not leave them in bewilderment, but offered them the remedy, their return to Him, for He alone is the secret of their healing from their incurable diseases. Repentance is not merely a turning back from sin; what is positive in it is the return to God and their constant preoccupation with Him.

Unable to perceive the truth of their depths they said: "Wherein shall we return?" They thought, while in their evil and their treachery against God and their weak brethren, that they were with God, and that He dwelt in their midst merely because of their care for Jerusalem and the presence of the Temple in it.

By saying "Wherein shall we return?" they declare what is in their hearts of murmuring against the true prophets, for they count them as those who love rebuke and demand things that are not their right, and who stir up their consciences without real cause. So in arrogance they say: Wherein shall we return? Or what are the sins that you attribute against us?

As He warns those who have no fear of the Lord and who mistreat their brethren, especially the weak, the poor, and the strangers, He assures them that His warning is irrevocable unless they move toward His mercy by turning back from what they are in, and clinging to the Lord Himself. By saying "For I am the LORD, I change not," He assures them that not one word of His falls to the ground. He does not appease sin, and does not accept fellowship with darkness. If in His longsuffering He bore with His people so that they were not consumed, it is only because He awaits their return to Him by repentance. He is faithful in His love and in His divine promises. He is "not a man, that he should lie" (Num 23:19).
As the prophet Jeremiah says: "It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not" (Lam 3:22-23).

The reply of Origen the Scholar to Celsus, who attacked Christianity as well as Judaism and claimed that the doctrine of the Incarnation makes God, by His condescension, subject to change from good to evil, from virtue to vice, from happiness to misery, and from what is better to what is worse. He says: [While continuing unchanged in His essence, He came down to human affairs by the economy of His providence. We show that the Holy Scripture presents God as unchangeable by saying: "Thou art the same" (Ps 102:27) and "I change not." Whereas the gods of Epicurus, being composed of atoms, are subject to dissolution as long as their being is so, and they seek, indeed drive out, the atoms that contain elements of destruction. Even the god of the Stoics, being material, at one time has his whole substance consisting of the primary ruling element, when the world is consumed by fire. At another time, when things are reorganized, he becomes partly material. Even the Stoics were unable to grasp naturally the idea of God in a distinctive way, as a being entirely incorruptible, simple, and indivisible.

* Hear God saying: "I am he, I am he, I change not." He remains always constant and unchanging in His being, and those who are formed by the Gospel, and who have been changed by His commandments as far as they are able, will not turn aside from that in which they live through time. For this reason Paul also warns the people: "Be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God" (Rom 12:2).

St. Severus of Antioch * How can he be subject to change and alteration who says: "I am in the Father, and the Father in me" (Jn 14:10), and "I and my Father are one" (Jn 10:30), and by the prophet: "I am the LORD, I change not" (Mal 3:6)...? When He became man He did not change, but as the Apostle says: "Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever" (Heb 13:8).
Pope Alexander of Alexandria * God remains always as He is, and does not stand in need of progress, He who is always as He is, from Himself and to Himself.

St. Hilary of Poitiers * The creature is changed by the Creator as He pleases, for it is changeable and obeys the nod of Him who created it. But the Creator's nature is constant and unchangeable, therefore the prophet says of the nature of the Creator: [He is the maker of all things and the one who changes them] (cf. Amos 5:8) LXX. And of the divine Word the great David says: "Thou art the same, and thy years shall have no end" (Ps 102:27). Again God Himself says of Himself: "I am the LORD, I change not" (Mal 3:6).

* If by nature He is higher than change and alteration, then He does not pass from being incapable of death to being mortal, nor from being incapable of suffering to feeling suffering, for if this were possible there would have been no need for Him to take our nature.

Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrus * We need what the Apostle says: "And be renewed in the spirit of your mind" (Eph 4:23), and spiritual progress, for "forgetting those things which are behind" (Phil 3:13). If a person neglects to do so, the inevitable result is relapse and retreat from bad to worse.

The mind cannot remain in one state. Just as a man who rows strongly tries to resist with his boat against the strong storm, forcing his way through the current by the strength of his arms, and so presses on to what is ahead, but if he relaxes his hands, his boat turns quickly under the force of the storm, so our failure becomes clear if we gain nothing more. For without doubt we fall back when we are not advancing forward.

And as I said, the human mind cannot remain as it is, for no saint can reach the heights of all the virtues as long as he remains in the flesh, if he remains unchanged. Either he adds something or loses something. We confess that God alone is unchangeable, so the blessed prophet prays to Him saying: "But thou art the same, and thy years shall not fail" (Heb 1:12). And God says of Himself: "I am the LORD, I change not" (Mal 3:6). For He alone is by nature always good and wholly good, and nothing can be added to Him or taken from Him.

Therefore we must submit to the demands of virtue with great care and eagerness, and occupy ourselves with its work, because, as we said, the mind cannot remain in one state, that is, it cannot remain without its good qualities being increased or decreased. Failure to acquire new qualities means that there is a loss. And when the desire for progress ceases, there is danger of falling back.

Father Theodore * The Savior Himself says: "Behold, here am I, I change not" (Mal 3:6), while Paul writes: "Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever" (Heb 13:8), yet in the flesh He was circumcised, and carried, and ate and drank, and was troubled, and was hanged on a tree and suffered, and in Him was the Word of God, who is not subject to immaterial suffering.

* If (the Arians) slander thus by ascribing change to the Word, let them learn how great is the danger in their thought, for "the tree is known by his fruit" (Mt 12:23). And for this also: "He that hath seen me hath seen the Father" (Jn 14:9). And for this also the knowledge of the Son is also the knowledge of the Father. Therefore the unchanging image of God must be constant and unchanging, for "Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever" (Heb 12:8). And David says singing of Him: "Thou, Lord, in the beginning hast laid the foundation of the earth; and the heavens are the works of thine hands: They shall perish; but thou remainest; and they all shall wax old as doth a garment; and as a vesture shalt thou fold them up, and they shall be changed: but thou art the same, and thy years shall not fail" (Ps 102:26-28; Heb 12:10-12). And the Lord Himself says of Himself by the prophet: "See now that I, even I, am he" (Deut 32:39), and also: "I change not" (Mal 3:6). And perhaps someone will say that the Father is meant here. But it is fitting that this be said of the Son also. Especially since when He becomes man, He shows His person as it is, and shows His unchangeableness, for the sake of those who imagine that since He took a body, He has changed and become another... The nature of all creatures and all beings is changeable and alterable, and by excluding the Son from them, (Scripture) shows concerning Him by saying: "Thou art the same, and thy years shall not fail" (Heb 1:12). He (the Son) does not alter and does not change. And this is rightly natural. For created things, since they arose from nothing, and since they were not before they were created, therefore have a changeable nature, since in general they were created from nothing. But the Son is from the Father and is of the same essence as the Father, therefore it is not right for anyone to say that from the essence of the Unchangeable is born a changeable word, and a wisdom subject to alteration.

* Aaron had successors, and in general the men of the priesthood according to the Law take the place of their predecessors in time or because of death. But the Lord has "an unchangeable priesthood" (cf. Heb 7:24). He has become a faithful high priest abiding forever, and He became faithful according to the promise, so as to answer those who draw near to Him and not deceive them. And this you can learn from: "Let them that suffer according to the will of God commit the keeping of their souls to him in well doing, as unto a faithful Creator" (1 Pet 4:19), for He is faithful and unchangeable, but is constant forever, and He gives those things which He promised.
St. Athanasius the Apostolic

entries.section: 4. Returning to the LORD of hosts:

paragraphs.text: 7 "Even from the days of your fathers ye are gone away from mine ordinances, and have not kept them. Return unto me, and I will return unto you, saith the LORD of hosts. But ye said, Wherein shall we return? 8 Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me. But ye say, Wherein have we robbed thee? In tithes and offerings. 9 Ye are cursed with a curse: for ye have robbed me, even this whole nation. 10 Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it. 11 And I will rebuke the devourer for your sakes, and he shall not destroy the fruits of your ground; neither shall your vine cast her fruit before the time in the field, saith the LORD of hosts. 12 And all nations shall call you blessed: for ye shall be a delightsome land, saith the LORD of hosts.
Even from the days of your fathers ye are gone away from mine ordinances, and have not kept them.
Return unto me, and I will return unto you, saith the LORD of hosts.
But ye said, Wherein shall we return? [7]

The Jews were occupied with offerings and sacrifices and their abundance, without caring for purity of heart and the practice of brotherly love, especially toward the needy. Therefore He declares to them that returning to Him with a living, practical faith must be realized through His poor brethren, "the brethren of the Lord," and as the beloved St. John says: "For he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen?" (1 Jn 4:20).

* While (the wicked man) angers God by his many and continual transgressions, God is longsuffering toward him, and in His longsuffering awaits the day of judgment, so that all may make up their minds (to repent)... He prefers to be longsuffering toward him for a long time, bearing with him in mercy, postponing (his punishment),... awaiting his return to Him, just as God Himself counsels us, saying: "For I have no pleasure in the death of him that dieth, saith the Lord GOD: wherefore turn yourselves, and live ye" (Ezek 18:32). Again: "Return unto me, saith the LORD of hosts" (cf. Mal 3:7).

St. Cyprian the Martyr * Seek the Lord, O sinners, and be strengthened in your thoughts because of hope. Seek His face by repentance at all times (Ps 105:3), and you will be sanctified by the holiness of His presence, and cleansed from your iniquities (Ezek 36:25). Hasten to the Lord, O sinners, for He blots out iniquity and removes sins. For He has sworn: "I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked" (Ezek 33:11), but that the sinner repent and live. [I have spread out my hands all the day unto a rebellious and disobedient people] (cf. Isa 65:2). "Why will ye die, O house of Israel?" (Ps 33:11). "Return unto me, and I will return unto you" (Mal 3:7).

St. Isaac the Syrian * Thou hadst a whore's forehead, thou refusedst to be ashamed (Jer 3:3). Return, O wretched one, to the Lord, and He will return to you [7]. Repent, and He will repent of the evil (the chastisement) which He was about to bring upon you.
St. Jerome Will a man rob God?
Yet ye have robbed me.
But ye say, Wherein have we robbed thee?

entries.section: 4. Returning to the LORD of hosts:

paragraphs.text: In tithes and offerings. [8]
The Lord Himself answers their question: "Ye have robbed me"] 8[This is a new accusation directed by the Lord Himself against the people through the prophet.
The first accusation: the priests' contempt for the name of the Lord (Mal 1:6).
The second accusation: they offer polluted bread upon the altar of the Lord (Mal 1:7).
The third accusation: they caused many to stumble at the Law, they corrupted the covenant of God (Mal 3:8).
The fourth accusation: treachery and the doing of an abomination in Israel and in Jerusalem (Mal 3:11).
The fifth accusation: they wearied the Lord with their words (Mal 3:17).
The sixth accusation: from the days of their fathers they turned aside from His ordinances and did not keep them (Mal 3:7).
The seventh accusation: they robbed the Lord (Mal 3:8).
The eighth accusation: their words have been stout against the Lord (Mal 3:13).

Here the seventh accusation is presented, which is an accusation of robbing the Lord by force, and taking away His rights over them. How can a weak creature rob God, who owns the world and everything, the Almighty? Does he imagine that he robs Him secretly without His knowledge or without His ability to resist? It is folly for a man to commit such a crime against God.
"But ye say, Wherein have we robbed thee?" In boldness they justify themselves and ask God for proof that they committed this crime.

They robbed Him of the tithes of what He gave them freely, and of what they had vowed, and of the offerings prescribed in the Law. And by this they committed a crime against the whole nation, since the poor, the needy, and the destitute find no share for themselves in the house of the Lord. Moreover, since they acted stingily toward the house of God, the curse came upon the land, and the nation lost many of the good things and divine gifts because of this curse. Famines and plagues came, and nature rose up against man!

He had already chastened them with the same chastening when they were concerned with building their own houses and ignored the building of the house of the Lord (Hag 1:10-11), and now He repeats the chastening because they did not provide for the needs of the service in the Temple.

entries.section: 4. Returning to the LORD of hosts:

paragraphs.text: Ye are cursed with a curse: for ye have robbed me, even this whole nation. [9]

entries.section: 4. Returning to the LORD of hosts:

paragraphs.text: Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it. [10]

He gives them sincere advice so that they may experience in practice how generous giving opens before them the windows of heaven. He refers to the divine gifts as though from heaven, from where man did not expect, flowing upon him suddenly without expectation.
God in His love and generosity does not stop at reconciliation with the man who returns to Him, but pours out on him more than he can imagine!

entries.section: 4. Returning to the LORD of hosts:

paragraphs.text: And I will rebuke the devourer for your sakes, and he shall not destroy the fruits of your ground; neither shall your vine cast her fruit before the time in the field, saith the LORD of hosts. [11]
God removes from them the plague of "locusts" and the insects that ruin the fields, so that they no longer find a spoiled vine in their fields.

entries.section: 4. Returning to the LORD of hosts:

paragraphs.text: And all nations shall call you blessed: for ye shall be a delightsome land, saith the LORD of hosts. [12]

Along with material gifts they receive esteem and respect from all the nations, as the peoples sense the Lord's delight in them, and call them blessed after they had become the object of the peoples' mockery because of their sins; even their land becomes a "delightsome land." As the Lord says: "This is my rest for ever: here will I dwell; for I have desired it" (Ps 132:14).

* The Lord God is not in need; He does not seek a reward, but honor. He does not ask you to return to Him anything from your own. He asks for the firstfruits and the tithes, and will you refuse? This indeed happened when the harvest became meager because of drought of rain, and when hail struck your vineyards and frost destroyed them. Why did this happen but because of your greedy reckonings? He took nine-tenths from you, because you refused to pay the tithes... You will give to the wicked soldier (through captivity or the violence he practices) what you refuse to give to the priest... God is always ready to bestow good things, but the evil of humanity prevents it, because man wants to receive everything from the Lord God, and does not want to offer anything of what he thinks he owns. Now imagine that God says: "Of course you are mine, O man, for I created you. The land you till and the seeds you sow are mine. The animals you use are mine, and also the rain and the breaths of the winds and the heat of the sun are mine. Since all the elements of life are mine, and you have only laid your hands on them, you deserve merely the tithes." Now although Almighty God in His tenderness feeds us, and gives man an abundant reward for his small labor, He demands the tithes for Himself and leaves all the rest to us.
Father Caesarius, Bishop of Arles

13 "Your words have been stout against me, saith the LORD. Yet ye say, What have we spoken so much against thee? 14 Ye have said, It is vain to serve God: and what profit is it that we have kept his ordinance, and that we have walked mournfully before the LORD of hosts? 15 And now we call the proud happy; yea, they that work wickedness are set up; yea, they that tempt God are even delivered."
Your words have been stout against me, saith the LORD.
Yet ye say, What have we spoken so much against thee? [13]

As the people were occupied with material wealth, they looked among themselves and saw the wicked rich and the proud occupying positions of leadership, so they counted what they had offered in their worship of offerings and sacrifices as worthless, and perhaps even counted it a loss. They lost what they offered to the Temple and received nothing, but rather trials came upon them and sorrow prevailed among them.

Here He presents the eighth accusation, which is that their words have been stout against the Lord, and some translate it as words that are bold against the Lord. In boldness without reverence they spoke against the Lord, and objected to Him, and counted worship of Him a waste of time and money, and an entry into a state of sorrow and bitterness.

They denied what they had said, whether openly or secretly, with their mouths or with their minds and thoughts. "What have we spoken against thee?" They asked the prophet to produce proof of this accusation directed against them. Perhaps here they do not deny what they said, but they counted it a trifling matter not worthy of the prophet's uproar against them. As though they were saying: What we said is counted as nothing compared with what the pagan nations said against the Lord, and the evils we practiced are counted as nothing compared with the evils of the nations, so why all this uproar?

They did not endure the words of rebuke, and instead of looking into their depths, to ask the Lord to cleanse and sanctify them, they compared themselves with other nations and counted themselves righteous and good. For this reason the Apostle Paul asks us to compare spiritual things with spiritual (1 Cor 2:13).
Ye have said, It is vain to serve God.
And what profit is it that we have kept his ordinance, and that we have walked mournfully before the LORD of hosts? [14]
And now we call the proud happy; yea, they that work wickedness are set up.
Yea, they that tempt God are even delivered. [15]

As they compared themselves with the pagan nations, they counted worship of God vain, since it brought them to sorrow, while the proud pagans who refuse to believe in the living God, and the workers of evil, live in surpassing happiness, building and growing and lacking nothing. They call the wicked blessed and regret their clinging to the Lord and worshiping Him, as though He were a source of sorrow and gloom.

These did not realize that the cause of their sorrow and unhappiness is not the worship of God, but that they teach as doctrines the commandments of men (Mt 15:9), and that they draw near to the Lord with their lips while their hearts are far from Him (Mt 15:8). They did not realize that the secret of their misery is their attachment to earthly gifts and temporal comfort. As the Apostle Paul says: "If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are of all men most miserable" (1 Cor 15:19). But he who worships the Lord in spirit and with heavenly wisdom realizes that "her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace" (Prov 3:17).

* This is what the prophet proclaims about the last judgment, in which the wicked will not be happy even in appearance, but will clearly be in utmost misery, while the righteous will not suffer any distress or misery, even temporary, but will enjoy complete, eternal happiness. He had previously quoted similar expressions about these men, when he said: "Every one that doeth evil is good in the sight of the LORD, and he delighteth in them" (Mal 2:17). I say this happens because of understanding the Law of Moses in a carnal way, therefore they murmured against God.

* Those who are spiritually immature place their trust more in temporal promises, and serve God looking to such rewards. For when the wicked prosper they are greatly troubled. Therefore Malachi continues, for their enlightenment, distinguishing between the eternal blessings of the New Testament, which the righteous alone receive, and the bare temporal blessings of the Old Testament, which the wicked often do not receive. He says: "Your words have been stout against me, saith the LORD. Yet ye say, What have we spoken so much against thee? Ye have said, It is vain to serve God: and what profit is it that we have kept his ordinance, and that we have walked mournfully before the LORD of hosts? And now we call the proud happy; yea, they that work wickedness are set up; yea, they that tempt God are even delivered" (Mal 3:13-15).

* "We call the proud happy; yea, they that work wickedness are set up" (Mal 3:14-15). Such complaints drove the prophet to ask for the hastening of the last judgment, in which the wicked will be far from pretending to happiness, for their misery will be evident to all. The righteous, no longer troubled by passing sorrows, will enjoy a clear, infinite blessedness. Malachi gave a similar explanation to those who by their murmuring vex the Lord: "Every one that doeth evil (thinks) he is good in the sight of the LORD, and that He delighteth in such." The only point I wish to stress is that such murmurings against God are the fruit of the non-spiritual interpretation of the Law.

St. Augustine * I beg you to contemplate the virtue of the righteous man (Malachi) and the arrogance of the Jews. He who feels that there is no sin in him pronounces a very harsh sentence on himself when he says: "We have sinned, we have walked as rebels against the Law, we have done evil." But those who were filled with myriads of evils did the opposite when they said: "We have kept it, glorifying" (Mal 3:14-15) LXX. The righteous usually walk in meekness after practicing what is good, and the wicked in general glorify themselves after they sin... I say this so that we may avoid the sinner and imitate the righteous.
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: 6. His dealing with them as sons:

paragraphs.text: 16 Then they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD, and that thought upon his name. 17 "And they shall be mine, saith the LORD of hosts, in that day when I make up my jewels; and I will spare them, as a man spareth his own son that serveth him. 18 Then shall ye return, and discern between the righteous and the wicked, between him that serveth God and him that serveth him not.

Returning to God does not stop at giving to the brethren of the Lord, nor at the spiritual understanding of the concept of worship, but it befits the believers to realize the truth of God as a Father who has compassion on them as His children; thus they enjoy the spirit of discernment, so they distinguish the righteous who live the life of sonship to God, and the wicked who disobey the heavenly Father.

Then they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD, and that thought upon his name. [16]

Having presented the view of the worshipers of the Lord who worship in a literal, deadly way with corrupt conduct, so that they saw it as a source of sorrow, he now presents to us the view of those who fear the Lord and revere Him and think upon His name. Here he links godliness, or the fear of the Lord, with constant preoccupation with God. For those who bear the fear of the Lord as loving sons fear to wound their relationship with Him, so all their thoughts, feelings, senses, and emotions are absorbed in the Lord and in His name, sweet in their inner mouths.

Those who have this sweet spiritual experience will not cease to bear witness to the name of the Lord and His saving work. "And spake often one to another," for "out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh" (Mt 12:34). "A good man out of the good treasure of the heart bringeth forth good things" (Mt 12:35).
The spiritual man speaks, not only with his lips and tongue, but by his conduct, his thoughts, and his features, bearing witness to the Kingdom of God dwelling in him.

How wonderful are his words: "And the LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him," for He longs for the speech of those who love Him, His pious ones; He listens to them and hears the words of their hearts, and records as in a book of remembrance, esteeming every word they utter. The heavenly Bridegroom says to the human soul sanctified in Him: "Thou hast ravished my heart, my sister, my spouse; thou hast ravished my heart with one of thine eyes" (Song 4:9); "Let me hear thy voice, let me see thy countenance; for sweet is thy voice, and thy countenance is comely" (Song 2:14).

"And a book of remembrance was written before him": this is a human expression that reveals to us in our language God's esteem for the words of His children and their holy thoughts, their tears and the sighs of their hearts. As the psalmist says: "Put thou my tears into thy bottle: are they not in thy book?" (Ps 56:8).

* He says this not as though there were a book on high and people writing, but by the book he means precious and precise knowledge, as he says: "The LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book...was written," and also "the books were opened" (Dan 7:10).

entries.section: 6. His dealing with them as sons:

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom And they shall be mine, saith the LORD of hosts, in that day when I make up my jewels; and I will spare them, as a man spareth his own son that serveth him. [17]

God esteems not only the words of those who fear Him, their thoughts and feelings, but He esteems their persons, and ascribes them to Himself as His children: "They shall be mine, saith the LORD of hosts." He counts them His own treasure, "when I make up my jewels" (lit. "I make His own"), so He calls Himself: "I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." He is the God of every person who counts God as his own, and so is God's own. Whoever esteems God and glorifies Him, God esteems him and pours the splendor of His glory into his depths.

As the Lord Himself says: "And will be the glory in the midst of her" (Zech 2:5). "As the bridegroom rejoiceth over the bride, so shall thy God rejoice over thee" (Isa 62:5). "Thou shalt also be a crown of glory in the hand of the LORD, and a royal diadem in the hand of thy God" (Isa 62:3).

entries.section: 6. His dealing with them as sons:

paragraphs.text: Then shall ye return, and discern between the righteous and the wicked, between him that serveth God and him that serveth him not. [18]

Since the Lord accepts from those who fear Him the least services and esteems them because they come from His own, from His children beloved to Him, He gives the finest gift, which is the knowledge that flows from Him. He gives them the spirit of discernment, so that by His Spirit they distinguish between the righteous and the wicked, and between him that serveth God and him that serveth Him not, a matter which belongs to God, the Knower of hearts.

* Now the proud are called happy; yes, those who tempt God are delivered. But the Lord afterward threatens them with the day of judgment, and announces beforehand the distinction that will take place between the righteous and the wicked, saying to them thus: "Then shall ye return, and discern between the righteous and the wicked, between him that serveth God and him that serveth him not" (Mal 3:18).
St. Jerome
Purify my depths and dwell in them, O Holy One!
* You sent St. John the Baptist as Your messenger, to prepare the way before You by proclaiming repentance!
You gave me Your Holy Spirit, who grants me adoption.
In the waters of Baptism You raised me to the bosom of Your Father, and presented me as a son who bears Your marvelous righteousness!
What shall I render to You before this surpassing love?
* Dwell, O Lord, in my depths, O consuming Fire, burning up all the thorns that choke my soul, and make of me a fiery being, whom all the waters of the world cannot quench.
Sanctify me, purify me, that I may become an icon of You, O You who alone are Holy!
* I see You coming down to my weakness; I long to return to You, O true Love!

You come to me through the suffering, the sick, and the needy, for You are the Father of the fatherless, the Judge of the widows, and the Shepherd of straying souls, to bring them back to Your marvelous pastures!
* Grant me also to worship You as You desire.
I worship You in spirit and in truth, that I may rise above the letter, and enjoy the Spirit!
Grant me the wings of the Spirit, that I may fly to You, rise above all earthly things, and ask nothing of the temporal.
* Finally grant me the spirit of discernment, that I may know that You are my Father.
I see even in Your chastenings a fatherhood, tenderness, and heavenly care.
I distinguish righteousness from evil, and I am in touch with Your righteous saints, and I do not take part with the wicked deceivers.

1 "For, behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the LORD of hosts, that it shall leave them neither root nor branch.

In the previous chapter he spoke of the spirit of discernment by which we realize that God is our Father, for He has compassion on us as His children, and sent His Word incarnate to unite us to Himself by our return through the work of His grace. But it is also fitting to realize that He is the Holy One who does not appease sin, but burns it as in an oven (furnace). He came to stretch out His hands in love to all humanity, but if a man insists on the pride of his heart and does evil, he casts himself under eternal judgment and perishes.

For, behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the LORD of hosts, that it shall leave them neither root nor branch. [1]

The prophet Malachi prophesies about the day of the coming of the incarnate Word to accomplish salvation, for although He stretches out His arms to all humanity, He came to send fire. Whoever believes in Him enjoys eternal life, but he who exalts himself against Him and rejects Him burns like stubble in the midst of the fire. This is what the psalmist prophesied about the Messiah: "Thou shalt make them as a fiery oven in the time of thine anger: the LORD shall swallow them up in his wrath, and the fire shall devour them" (Ps 21:9).

God, who knows the hearts, alone is able to separate the stubble from the gold, the proud from the humble. The former are counted workers of evil who burn in the fire, so that He leaves them neither root nor branch, and the latter increase in splendor and purity.
